```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = here::here())
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, message = FALSE, warning = FALSE,
                      fig.align = "center", fig.pos = "!htbp",
                      fig.topcaption = TRUE)
library(here)

# ---- Results (the only source of data-derived numbers) ----------------------
res <- function(f) readRDS(here("outputs", "results", f))
s1 <- res("01_summary_table.rds")    # Table 1: group-year aggregates
ct <- res("02_country_table.rds")    # Table 2: country classification
br <- res("03_fig_break.rds")        # Figure 1
bt <- res("04_fig_brent.rds")        # Figure 2
im <- res("05_fig_impact.rds")       # Figure 3
m  <- res("06_model.rds")            # Table 3 and Figure 4
fa <- res("07_fiscal_analysis.rds")  # Table 6 and Figure 5
rb <- res("08_robustness.rds")       # Table 4
cs <- res("09_classification_sensitivity.rds")  # classification sensitivity table
clf <- res("classification.rds")     # treatment classification (UN Comtrade)

# Panels, used only for sample coverage facts
panel <- readxl::read_excel(here("data", "processed", "panel_country_year.xlsx"))
wb    <- read.csv(here("data", "raw", "fiscal_wb.csv"))
weo   <- readxl::read_excel(here("data", "raw", "fiscal_weo.xlsx"))
oiltr <- read.csv(here("data", "raw", "oil_trade_comtrade.csv"))   # HS breakdown of switches

# ---- Formatting helpers ------------------------------------------------------
minus <- "\u2212"
num <- function(x, d = 2) {
  s <- formatC(abs(x), format = "f", digits = d, big.mark = ",")
  ifelse(round(x, d) < 0, paste0(minus, s), s)
}
sgn <- function(x, d = 2) ifelse(round(x, d) > 0, paste0("+", num(x, d)), num(x, d))
pp  <- function(x, d = 2) paste0(sgn(x, d), "\u00a0pp")    # signed, with unit
npp <- function(x, d = 2) paste0(num(x, d), "\u00a0pp")    # unsigned, with unit
fp  <- function(p) {
  if (p < 0.001) return("\\textit{p}\u00a0<\u00a00.001")
  paste0("\\textit{p}\u00a0=\u00a0", formatC(p, format = "f", digits = if (p < 0.01) 3 else 2))
}
fci <- function(lo, hi, d = 2) paste0("[", num(lo, d), ", ", num(hi, d), "]")
pct <- function(x, d = 0) paste0(num(100 * x, d), "%")
enum <- function(x) {
  if (length(x) <= 2) return(paste(x, collapse = " and "))
  paste0(paste(x[-length(x)], collapse = ", "), ", and ", x[length(x)])
}
the_c <- function(x) ifelse(x %in% c("Dominican Republic", "Bahamas"), paste("the", x), x)
nw <- function(n) {
  w <- c("zero", "one", "two", "three", "four", "five", "six", "seven", "eight",
         "nine", "ten")
  if (n >= 0 && n <= 10) w[n + 1] else as.character(n)
}
Nw <- function(n) { s <- nw(n); paste0(toupper(substr(s, 1, 1)), substr(s, 2, nchar(s))) }
ord <- function(n) c("first", "second", "third", "fourth", "fifth", "sixth",
                     "seventh", "eighth", "ninth", "tenth")[n]

# ---- Sample -----------------------------------------------------------------
smp    <- m$sample
n_c    <- smp$n_countries
n_exp  <- smp$n_exporters
n_imp  <- smp$n_importers
n_obs  <- smp$n_obs_panel
years  <- sort(unique(panel$anio))
y0 <- min(years); y1 <- max(years); n_years <- length(years)
exporters <- ct$net_exporters
pre_years <- years[years < 2022]
n_pre     <- length(pre_years)
base_year <- m$event_study_base_year
n_leads   <- sum(m$event_study$year < base_year)

# Missing values in the panel
miss_expl <- panel[is.na(panel$expl_pctgdp), c("pais", "anio")]
miss_expl_c <- unique(miss_expl$pais)
p_est <- panel[panel$anio <= 2022, ]
impl_cov <- tapply(p_est$impl_pctgdp, p_est$pais, function(v) sum(!is.na(v)))
impl_none <- sort(names(impl_cov)[impl_cov == 0])
impl_part <- sort(names(impl_cov)[impl_cov > 0 & impl_cov < 8])

# World Bank vs WEO coverage
wb_miss <- colMeans(is.na(wb[, c("balance_fiscal", "deuda_publica", "ingreso_publico")]))
weo_miss <- sum(is.na(weo[, c("balance_fiscal", "deuda_publica", "ingreso_publico")]))

# ---- Brent (Figure 2) --------------------------------------------------------
bs <- bt$series
b_diff <- diff(bs$brent_usd); names(b_diff) <- bs$year[-1]
b_pct  <- 100 * b_diff / head(bs$brent_usd, -1)
b_2021_pct <- b_pct[["2021"]]
b_2023 <- bs$brent_usd[bs$year == 2023]
stopifnot(names(which.max(b_diff)) == "2022",   # largest absolute annual rise
          names(which.max(bs$brent_usd)) == "2022")

# ---- Treatment classification (Section 2.4) ---------------------------------
cfv <- function(i, v) clf[[v]][clf$iso == i]
stopifnot(setequal(clf$country[clf$exportador_neto], exporters),
          cfv("VEN", "data_source") == "mirror",                 # Venezuela: mirror data
          cfv("PRI", "data_source") == "external",               # Puerto Rico: EIA exception
          !cfv("PRI", "exportador_neto"),
          all(clf$exportador_neto == (!is.na(clf$net_oil_trade_usd_1519) &
                                      clf$net_oil_trade_usd_1519 > 0)))
# Net trade by HS heading, 2015-2019 annual average (USD billion), from the raw Comtrade file
ot <- oiltr[oiltr$year %in% 2015:2019 & oiltr$cmd %in% c(2709, 2710, 2711), ]
ot$net <- ifelse(ot$flow == "X", 1, -1) * ot$value_usd
hs <- function(i, c) sum(ot$net[ot$iso == i & ot$cmd == c]) / 5 / 1e9
tto_y <- tapply(ot$net[ot$iso == "TTO" & ot$cmd %in% c(2709, 2710)],
                ot$year[ot$iso == "TTO" & ot$cmd %in% c(2709, 2710)], sum)
tto_neg <- as.integer(names(tto_y)[tto_y < 0]); tto_pos <- as.integer(names(tto_y)[tto_y > 0])
tto_avg_m <- cfv("TTO", "net_oil_trade_usd_1519") / 1e6
# switches relative to the previous hand-coded list
sw <- cs$switches$v5_manual
iso2c <- function(i) clf$country[match(i, clf$iso)]
stopifnot(setequal(sw$to_exporter, c("BOL", "GUY", "MEX")), setequal(sw$to_importer, "BRA"),
          all(unlist(lapply(c("MEX", "BOL", "BRA", "ARG", "TTO"), function(i)
            all(cfv(i, "n_years_1519") == 5, cfv(i, "data_source") == "own")))),
          # the HS recomputation reproduces the classification for these countries
          isTRUE(all.equal(hs("MEX", 2709) + hs("MEX", 2710), cfv("MEX", "net_oil_trade_usd_1519") / 1e9)),
          isTRUE(all.equal(hs("BRA", 2709) + hs("BRA", 2710), cfv("BRA", "net_oil_trade_usd_1519") / 1e9)),
          hs("MEX", 2709) > 0, -hs("MEX", 2710) > hs("MEX", 2709),     # Mexico: crude < refined imports
          hs("BOL", 2711) > 0, hs("BOL", 2711) > abs(hs("BOL", 2709)), # Bolivia: mainly gas
          -hs("BOL", 2710) > hs("BOL", 2709),                          # refined imports > crude exports
          hs("BRA", 2709) > -hs("BRA", 2710), hs("BRA", 2710) < 0,     # Brazil: crude > refined imports
          hs("ARG", 2709) > 0, -hs("ARG", 2710) > hs("ARG", 2709),     # Argentina: produces, net importer
          identical(tto_neg, c(2015L, 2016L)), identical(tto_pos, 2017:2019),  # TTO sign flips
          !cfv("GUY", "exportador_neto"), cfv("GUY", "exportador_1921"),
          cfv("GUY", "net_oil_trade_usd_1519") < 0, cfv("GUY", "net_oil_trade_usd_1921") > 0)

# ---- Descriptives (Table 1, Figure 1) ----------------------------------------
cg <- br$change_2021_2022
cgv <- function(g, v) cg[[v]][cg$group == g]
sy <- s1$by_group_year
syv <- function(g, y, v) sy[[v]][sy$group == g & sy$year == y]
# GDP-weighted aggregates: importers' subsidy rose slightly more (in pp) than exporters'
stopifnot(cgv("Net importer", "change_pp") > cgv("Net exporter", "change_pp"),
          cgv("Net exporter", "change_usd_bn") < cgv("Net importer", "change_usd_bn"),
          syv("Net importers", 2021, "explicit_pct_gdp") > syv("Net exporters", 2021, "explicit_pct_gdp"),
          all(sapply(c("Net exporters", "Net importers"), function(g)
            syv(g, 2022, "implicit_pct_gdp") > syv(g, 2021, "implicit_pct_gdp"))))
lac_s <- sy[sy$group == "LAC total" & sy$year < 2022, ]
stopifnot(lac_s$year[which.max(lac_s$explicit_pct_gdp)] == 2018,
          lac_s$year[which.min(lac_s$explicit_pct_gdp)] == 2020)

cl <- ct$classification
ven_y <- unlist(cl[cl$country == "Venezuela", grep("^explicit_pct_gdp_", names(cl))])
n_zero22 <- sum(round(cl$y2022, 2) <= im$floor_pct_gdp, na.rm = TRUE)
bra22 <- cl$y2022[cl$country == "Brazil"]
stopifnot(round(bra22, 2) <= im$floor_pct_gdp)          # Brazil among the near-zero countries

# ---- Figure 3 ----------------------------------------------------------------
imp <- im$impact[order(-im$impact$change_pp), ]
top3 <- head(imp, 3)
imv <- function(cn) imp$change_pp[imp$country == cn]
exp_ranked <- imp[imp$group == "Net exporter", ]
neg_exp <- exp_ranked$country[exp_ranked$change_pp < 0]
rank_of <- function(cn) which(imp$country == cn)
arg_rank <- rank_of("Argentina")
exp_below_arg <- sum(exp_ranked$change_pp < imv("Argentina"))
tiny_up <- imp$country[imp$change_pp > 0 & imp$change_pp < 0.005]
top3_alt <- head(cl$country[order(-cl$change_pp)], 3)   # 2015-2021 baseline (Table 2)
same_top3 <- setequal(top3$country, top3_alt)
top3_imp <- top3$country[top3$group == "Net importer"]
stopifnot(top3$group[1] == "Net importer", identical(neg_exp, "Brazil"),
          all(abs(unlist(cl[cl$country == "Brazil", grep("^explicit_pct_gdp_", names(cl))])) < 0.1))

# ---- Model (Table 3, Figure 4) -----------------------------------------------
tw <- m$twfe
rw <- function(mod) tw[tw$model == mod, ]
t1 <- rw("did_2x2"); t2 <- rw("twfe_explicit")
t3 <- rw("twfe_implicit_placebo"); t4 <- rw("twfe_total")
cells <- m$did_2x2_cells
cell <- function(g, p) cells$mean_subsidy[cells$group == g & cells$period == p]
cell_n <- function(g, p) cells$n_obs[cells$group == g & cells$period == p]
dd <- m$did_2x2
es <- m$event_study
es_pre <- es[es$year < base_year, ]
es22 <- es[es$year == 2022, ]; es23 <- es[es$year == 2023, ]
pre_cover0 <- es_pre$ci_low < 0 & es_pre$ci_high > 0
pre_excl0  <- es_pre[!pre_cover0, ]                       # leads whose CI excludes zero
n_pre_pos  <- sum(es_pre$coef > 0)
pre_neg    <- es_pre$year[es_pre$coef < 0]
b3_share   <- t2$coef / cell("Net exporter", "pre_2015_2021")
# qualitative claims made in the text
stopifnot(nrow(pre_excl0) == 1, pre_excl0$year == 2015, pre_excl0$ci_low > 0,
          cell("Net exporter", "pre_2015_2021") > cell("Net importer", "pre_2015_2021"),
          t2$coef > 0, t2$ci_low < 0, t2$p_value > 0.10,          # positive, not significant
          t2$ci_high > 2 * t2$coef,                               # CI admits effects > twice beta3
          t3$p_value > 0.10, t3$coef < 0, es23$ci_low < 0,
          es22$ci_low < 0, es22$coef == max(es$coef), es23$coef < es22$coef,
          t4$p_value > 0.10,
          es22$coef > t2$coef,                                    # delta_2022 > static beta3
          dd$importer_change > 0)                                  # importers' subsidy also rose

# Pre-trend test with G - 1 denominator degrees of freedom
wald <- m$pretrend_wald
wald_df2 <- wald$df2
wald_p   <- wald$p_value
stopifnot(wald_df2 == n_c - 1,                     # F(6, G - 1)
          wald_p > 0.10)                           # joint test does not reject

# Leads against the Brent price
lb <- merge(es[es$year <= base_year, c("year", "coef")], bs[, c("year", "brent_usd")], by = "year")
lp <- lb[lb$year < base_year, ]                               # the six leads only
r_leads_brent <- cor(lp$coef, lp$brent_usd)                    # 2015-2020
r_lead_brent  <- cor(lb$coef, lb$brent_usd)                    # incl. the 2021 reference zero
se_max_lead   <- max(es_pre$se)
lead_top  <- lp$year[which.max(lp$coef)]
d_top     <- lp$coef[which.max(lp$coef)]
brent_ref <- bs$brent_usd[bs$year == base_year]
brent_top <- bs$brent_usd[bs$year == lead_top]
d2022_vs_top <- es22$coef - d_top
stopifnot(r_leads_brent > 0.9, r_lead_brent < r_leads_brent,
          lead_top == lp$year[which.max(lp$brent_usd)],             # largest lead = highest-price lead year
          abs(brent_ref - brent_top) < 1,                           # 2021 Brent close to that year's
          n_pre_pos == n_leads - 1, identical(pre_neg, 2020L),
          se_max_lead > 0.5 * t2$coef,
          # 2021: importers rebounded more than exporters (aggregates)
          syv("Net importers", 2021, "explicit_pct_gdp") - syv("Net importers", 2020, "explicit_pct_gdp") >
            syv("Net exporters", 2021, "explicit_pct_gdp") - syv("Net exporters", 2020, "explicit_pct_gdp"))

# ---- Robustness (Table 4) ----------------------------------------------------
ex <- rb$exclusions
exr <- function(s) ex[ex$sample == s, ]
loo <- rb$leave_one_out
nven <- exr("without_venezuela")
stopifnot(all(loo$coef > 0), all(loo$p_value > 0.10), nven$p_value > 0.10,
          all(ex$p_value > 0.10),
          rb$loo_range$country_at_min == "Venezuela", rb$loo_range$country_at_max == "Brazil",
          exr("without_suriname")$coef > t2$coef)

# ---- Classification sensitivity (Table 5) ------------------------------------
vv  <- cs$variants
vk  <- function(k) vv[vv$variant == k, ]
bin <- vv[vv$variant %in% c(1:5, 7, 8), ]                  # binary definitions
bin_pre <- vv[vv$variant %in% 1:5, ]
ex_dist <- cs$exposure
ebc <- ex_dist$by_country
e_min_c <- ebc$country[which.min(ebc$net_oil_trade_gdp_1519)]
e_max_c <- ebc$country[which.max(ebc$net_oil_trade_gdp_1519)]
e_2nd_c <- ebc$country[ebc$iso == ex_dist$second_iso]
n_e_neg <- sum(ebc$net_oil_trade_gdp_1519 < 0)
cont_drop <- 1 - vk(9)$coef / vk(6)$coef
bol_ch <- cl$change_pp[cl$country == "Bolivia"]
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(vk(1)$coef, t2$coef)), isTRUE(all.equal(vk(1)$p_value, t2$p_value)),
          all(vv$type[vv$variant %in% 1:6] == "pre-specified"),
          all(vv$type[vv$variant %in% 7:9] == "post hoc"),
          all(bin$coef > 0), all(bin$p_value > 0.05),              # sign robust, not significance
          sum(bin$p_value < 0.10) == 2, all(which(bin$p_value < 0.10) %in% which(bin$variant %in% c(2, 5))),
          which.max(bin$coef) == which(bin$variant == 2),
          which.min(bin$coef) == which(bin$variant == 3),
          vk(5)$p_value < 0.10, vk(5)$coef > t2$coef,
          vk(6)$p_value < 0.001, vk(9)$p_value < 0.05, vk(9)$coef > 0, vk(9)$coef < vk(6)$coef,
          identical(cs$switches$v2_gas$to_exporter, "BOL"),
          identical(cs$switches$v3_1921$to_exporter, "GUY"),
          identical(cs$excluded$v9, c("PRI", "VEN")),
          e_max_c == "Venezuela", ex_dist$second_iso == "ECU",
          ex_dist$max > 4 * ex_dist$second,
          ex_dist$median < 0,
          vk(4)$coef > 0 && abs(vk(4)$coef - t2$coef) < 0.1,
          bol_ch == sort(cl$change_pp, decreasing = TRUE)[2])       # Bolivia: 2nd-largest rise

# ---- Fiscal matrix (Table 6, Figure 5) ---------------------------------------
fc  <- fa$countries
fcv <- function(cn, v) fc[[v]][fc$country == cn]
qc  <- fa$quadrant_countries
urg <- fc[fc$quadrant == "Urgent reform", ]
urg_exp <- urg$country[urg$group == "Net exporter"]
urg_imp <- urg$country[urg$group == "Net importer"]
urg_def <- urg[urg$fiscal_balance_pct_gdp_2022 < 0, ]
urg_def <- urg_def[order(urg_def$fiscal_balance_pct_gdp_2022), ]
# Illustrative differential cost: beta3 (and its 95% CI) x 2022 GDP, exporters in the matrix
fx <- fc[fc$group == "Net exporter", ]
fx$cost    <- fx$shock_cost_usd_bn
fx$cost_lo <- fx$shock_cost_low_usd_bn
fx$cost_hi <- fx$shock_cost_high_usd_bn
fx <- fx[order(-fx$cost), ]
exp_out <- setdiff(exporters, fx$country)                 # exporters below the subsidy floor
stopifnot(!anyNA(fx$cost), isTRUE(all.equal(fa$beta3$coef, t2$coef)),
          nrow(fx) == fa$n_exporters, identical(exp_out, "Brazil"),
          bra22 < fa$subsidy_floor_pct_gdp,
          fx$country[1] == "Colombia",
          all(c("Suriname", "Bolivia", "Argentina") %in% urg_imp),
          all(sapply(qc[["Monitor"]], function(x) x %in% fc$country[fc$group == "Net importer"])))
fxv <- function(cn, v) fx[[v]][fx$country == cn]
# Countries close to the quadrant cut-offs
band_debt <- 5; band_sub <- 0.1
near_med <- fc$country[abs(fc$debt_pct_gdp_2022 - fa$median_debt_pct_gdp) < band_debt |
                       abs(fc$explicit_subsidy_pct_gdp_2022 - fa$median_subsidy_pct_gdp) < band_sub]
near_med <- sort(near_med)
stopifnot(all(fx$cost_lo < 0))                           # lower end of every range negative

# Other qualitative claims in the text
g22 <- panel[panel$anio == 2022, ]
stopifnot(g22$pais[g22$exportador_neto][which.max(g22$gdp[g22$exportador_neto])] == "Brazil",
          g22$pais[!g22$exportador_neto][which.max(g22$gdp[!g22$exportador_neto])] == "Mexico",
          cl$change_pp[cl$country == "Mexico"] > 0,
          cl$change_pp[cl$country == "Brazil"] < 0,
          abs(vk(7)$coef - t2$coef) < 0.1, abs(vk(8)$coef - t2$coef) < 0.35)

# ---- Figures: outputs/figures/* with notes from figure_notes.rds ------------
fig_notes <- res("figure_notes.rds")
tex_escape <- function(x) {
  x <- gsub("\\", "\001", x, fixed = TRUE)            # protect backslashes
  x <- gsub("([&%$#_{}])", "\\\\\\1", x)              # & % $ # _ { }
  x <- gsub("~", "\\textasciitilde{}", x, fixed = TRUE)
  x <- gsub("^", "\\textasciicircum{}", x, fixed = TRUE)
  gsub("\001", "\\textbackslash{}", x, fixed = TRUE)
}
# typographic clean-up for text coming from the pipeline (after escaping)
tex_typo <- function(x) {
  x <- gsub("(?<![0-9A-Za-z])-(?=[0-9.])", "\u2212", x, perl = TRUE)   # minus sign
  x <- gsub("([0-9]{4})-([0-9]{2,4})", "\\1\u2013\\2", x)               # year ranges
  x <- gsub("\u03b2\u2083", "$\\\\beta_3$", x)                          # beta_3
  x <- gsub("\u03b2", "$\\\\beta$", x)
  x
}
fig_float <- function(file, caption, label, width = "\\linewidth",
                      max_height = "0.62\\textheight") {
  stem <- tools::file_path_sans_ext(file)
  cand <- here("outputs", "figures", paste0(stem, c(".pdf", ".png")))
  path <- cand[file.exists(cand)][1]
  stopifnot(!is.na(path))
  nt <- fig_notes[[basename(path)]]
  if (is.null(nt)) nt <- fig_notes[[file]]
  if (is.null(nt)) nt <- fig_notes[[paste0(stem, ".png")]]
  if (is.null(nt)) nt <- fig_notes[[paste0(stem, ".pdf")]]
  stopifnot(!is.null(nt))
  txt <- paste0("\\emph{Notes:} ", tex_typo(tex_escape(nt$note)))
  if (!is.null(nt$source)) txt <- paste0(txt, " \\emph{Source:} ", tex_typo(tex_escape(nt$source)))
  cat("\n\\begin{figure}[!htbp]\n\\centering\n",
      "\\caption{", caption, "}\\label{fig:", label, "}\n",
      "\\includegraphics[width=", width, ",height=", max_height,
      ",keepaspectratio]{", path, "}\n",
      "\\par\\smallskip\n{\\footnotesize\\raggedright\\setstretch{1}\\noindent ", txt,
      "\\par}\n\\end{figure}\n\n", sep = "")
}

# ---- Tables: native booktabs tables from outputs/tables/*.xlsx ---------------
# xlsx layout: row 1 title (ignored; caption comes from here), row 2 header,
# optional row 3 sub-header (empty first cell), body, last non-empty cell of
# column 1 = notes ("Notes. ...").
tab_cell <- function(x) {
  x <- tex_typo(tex_escape(x))
  ifelse(grepl("\n", x, fixed = TRUE),
         paste0("\\makecell{", gsub("\n", "\\\\", x, fixed = TRUE), "}"), x)
}
tab_float <- function(file, caption, label, size = "\\footnotesize",
                      colsep = NULL, landscape = FALSE) {
  d <- openxlsx::read.xlsx(here("outputs", "tables", file), colNames = FALSE,
                           skipEmptyRows = FALSE)
  d[] <- lapply(d, function(x) { x <- as.character(x); x[is.na(x)] <- ""; trimws(x) })
  d <- d[, vapply(d, function(x) any(x != ""), logical(1)), drop = FALSE]
  c1 <- d[[1]]
  nr <- max(which(c1 != ""))
  stopifnot(grepl("^Notes?[.:]", c1[nr]))
  note <- sub("^Notes?[.:]\\s*", "", c1[nr])
  note <- tex_typo(tex_escape(note))
  note <- sub("(^|\\s)Sources?:", "\\1\\\\emph{Source:}", note)
  hdr  <- unlist(d[2, ])
  body <- d[3:(nr - 1), , drop = FALSE]
  body <- body[apply(body, 1, function(r) any(r != "")), , drop = FALSE]
  sub_hdr <- NULL
  if (body[1, 1] == "") { sub_hdr <- unlist(body[1, ]); body <- body[-1, , drop = FALSE] }
  nc <- length(hdr)
  has_panels <- any(grepl("^Panel ", body[[1]]))
  row_tex <- function(r) paste0(paste(tab_cell(r), collapse = " & "), " \\\\")
  out <- c("\\toprule", row_tex(hdr))
  if (!is.null(sub_hdr)) out <- c(out, row_tex(sub_hdr))
  out <- c(out, "\\midrule")
  ruled <- TRUE; prev_fe <- FALSE
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(body))) {
    r <- unlist(body[i, ]); f <- r[1]
    if (grepl("^Panel ", f)) {
      if (!ruled) out <- c(out, "\\midrule")
      out <- c(out, paste0("\\multicolumn{", nc, "}{@{}l}{\\textbf{", tab_cell(f), "}} \\\\"))
      ruled <- FALSE; prev_fe <- FALSE; next
    }
    is_n  <- grepl("^N( |$|\\()", f)
    is_fe <- grepl("FE$", f)
    if ((is_n || (is_fe && !prev_fe)) && !ruled) out <- c(out, "\\midrule")
    if (has_panels && !is_n && f != "") r[1] <- paste0("\\hspace{0.6em}", tab_cell(f)) else r[1] <- tab_cell(f)
    out <- c(out, paste0(paste(c(r[1], tab_cell(r[-1])), collapse = " & "), " \\\\"))
    ruled <- FALSE; prev_fe <- is_fe
  }
  out <- c(out, "\\bottomrule")
  spec <- paste0("@{}l", strrep("c", nc - 1), "@{}")
  cat("\n", if (landscape) "\\begin{landscape}\n",
      "\\begin{table}[!htbp]\n\\centering\n", size, "\n",
      if (!is.null(colsep)) paste0("\\setlength{\\tabcolsep}{", colsep, "}\n"),
      "\\caption{", caption, "}\\label{tab:", label, "}\n",
      "\\sbox{\\tabbox}{\\begin{tabular}{", spec, "}\n",
      paste(out, collapse = "\n"),
      "\n\\end{tabular}}\n",
      "\\typeout{TABWIDTH ", label, ": \\the\\wd\\tabbox\\space of \\the\\linewidth}\n",
      "\\ifdim\\wd\\tabbox>\\linewidth\\resizebox{\\linewidth}{!}{\\usebox{\\tabbox}}\\else\\usebox{\\tabbox}\\fi\n",
      "\\par\\smallskip\n{\\footnotesize\\raggedright\\setstretch{1}\\noindent \\emph{Notes:} ",
      note, "\\par}\n\\end{table}\n",
      if (landscape) "\\end{landscape}\n", "\n", sep = "")
}
```

\begin{abstract}
\noindent The rise in oil prices that began with the post-COVID-19 recovery in 2021 and intensified after the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022 was a common shock to every country in Latin America and the Caribbean. I use it to estimate whether explicit fossil fuel subsidies responded differently across countries depending on their net oil trade position, defined by a rule fixed before estimation: a country is a net oil exporter if its 2015--2019 net trade in crude oil and refined products (UN Comtrade) is positive. With a panel of `r n_c` countries over `r y0`--`r y1` from the IMF Fossil Fuel Subsidies Database and a two-way fixed effects difference-in-differences design, I estimate that the explicit subsidy of the `r nw(n_exp)` net oil exporters rose by `r num(t2$coef)` percentage points (pp) of GDP more than that of net importers in 2022 (clustered SE `r num(t2$se)`, `r fp(t2$p_value)`; 95\% CI `r fci(t2$ci_low, t2$ci_high)`). The estimate is not statistically significant, and it depends heavily on Venezuela: without it, the differential falls to `r npp(nven$coef)`. Point estimates are positive under every binary definition of exporters considered (`r num(min(bin$coef))` to `r npp(max(bin$coef))`), so the sign is robust but significance is not. A continuous measure of net oil exposure, pre-specified as a sensitivity check, points to a dose--response pattern (`r num(vk(6)$coef, 3)` pp of GDP per 1 pp of GDP of net oil exports), but it is heavily leveraged by Venezuela. A pre-trend test does not reject parallel trends (`r fp(wald_p)`), although it has little power. The evidence is suggestive, not conclusive. A descriptive subsidy--debt matrix shows that fiscal pressure is not confined to exporters: among the `r fa$n_countries` countries with non-negligible explicit subsidies, `r nw(nrow(urg))`, `r nw(length(urg_imp))` of them net importers, combine above-median subsidies with above-median public debt. I argue for a reform sequence differentiated by fiscal space, with targeted compensation replacing universal price subsidies.

\medskip
\noindent\textbf{JEL codes:} H23, H62, Q48, C23.\\
\noindent\textbf{Keywords:} fossil fuel subsidies, oil price shock, difference-in-differences, fiscal space, Latin America and the Caribbean.
\end{abstract}

\thispagestyle{empty}
\newpage

# Introduction

In 2022, the annual average price of Brent crude rose from USD `r num(bt$brent_2021, 1)` to USD `r num(bt$brent_2022, 1)` per barrel, an increase of `r num(bt$brent_pct_change_2021_2022, 0)`%. The increase began with the post-COVID-19 recovery in 2021 and intensified after the Russian invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, an event that was unexpected, global in scope, and unrelated to the subsidy decisions of any government in Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC). Worldwide, fossil fuel subsidies reached USD 7 trillion, or 7.1% of world GDP, in 2022, and explicit subsidies more than doubled relative to 2020 [@black2023imf]. Governments that hold domestic fuel prices below supply cost absorb international price increases in their budgets, so a shock of this size is also a fiscal event.

This paper asks how explicit fossil fuel subsidies in LAC responded to the 2022 shock and what that response implies for fiscal and subsidy policy. The starting point is that the same price increase operates through different channels depending on a country's net oil trade position. For a net oil exporter, a higher Brent price raises oil revenue, which makes it easier to keep the domestic price low: the subsidy expands, and there is rent to finance it. For a net importer, the higher price raises the cost of supply; if the consumer price is frozen, the subsidy also grows, but without additional revenue to back it. Because exporters have the rent to finance a larger price gap, I expect their explicit subsidy to rise more than importers', and more so the larger their net oil exposure (Section 4.1). Exporter status is also correlated with the degree of domestic price regulation, which, in turn, makes the explicit subsidy respond more to international prices. The design identifies a differential response by exporter status; it cannot separate the oil-rent channel from differences in pricing regimes.

That subsidies rose in 2022 is a descriptive fact, not an estimate of the shock's effect. I cannot observe what exporters' subsidies would have been without the shock, because every country in the region faced the same price increase. Instead, I compare how subsidies moved in net exporters with how they moved in net importers, which went through the same years, including the post-COVID-19 rebound and the 2022 inflation, and were exposed to the same price but not to the oil-rent channel. Netting out the change common to both groups yields a difference-in-differences (DiD) design, identified from the interaction between the shock year and exporter status. The resulting estimate is a *differential* effect: it measures how much more exporters' subsidies rose than importers', not the total effect of the shock on exporters.

The data combine the IMF Fossil Fuel Subsidies Database, which distinguishes between explicit and implicit subsidies [@imf2023ffsdata; @black2023imf], the EIA Brent price series [@eia2023brent], oil trade flows from UN Comtrade [@uncomtrade], and fiscal indicators from the IMF World Economic Outlook [@imf2023weo]. The panel covers `r n_c` LAC countries, `r nw(n_exp)` of them net oil exporters, over `r y0`--`r y1` (`r n_obs` country-years). Exporter status follows a data-based rule that I fixed before estimating any model; an earlier version of this analysis used a hand-coded list of exporters, which I now report only as a sensitivity check.

There are five main findings. First, the two-way fixed effects (TWFE) estimate implies that the explicit subsidy of net exporters rose by `r npp(t2$coef)` of GDP more than that of net importers in 2022, with a clustered standard error of `r num(t2$se)` (`r fp(t2$p_value)`; 95% CI `r fci(t2$ci_low, t2$ci_high)`). The point estimate is about `r pct(b3_share)` of the unweighted pre-shock mean of exporters (`r num(cell("Net exporter", "pre_2015_2021"))`% of GDP), but it is not statistically significant, and with only `r nw(n_exp)` treated countries, conventional clustered standard errors are, if anything, too small. Second, the estimate depends heavily on one country: without Venezuela, it falls to `r npp(nven$coef)` (`r fp(nven$p_value)`), and dropping each exporter in turn gives estimates between `r num(rb$loo_range$min)` and `r npp(rb$loo_range$max)`. Third, the sign is robust to how exporters are defined, but significance is not: across `r nw(nrow(bin))` binary definitions, the point estimate lies between `r num(min(bin$coef))` and `r npp(max(bin$coef))`, and none is significant at the 5% level; the earlier hand-coded list gives `r npp(vk(5)$coef)` (`r fp(vk(5)$p_value)`). Fourth, a continuous measure of net oil exposure points to a dose--response pattern: each additional percentage point of GDP in net oil exports is associated with a `r num(vk(6)$coef, 3)`\ pp larger differential (`r fp(vk(6)$p_value)`). This evidence is complementary and heavily leveraged by Venezuela, whose net oil exports equal `r num(ex_dist$max, 1)`% of GDP; without it, the slope falls to `r num(vk(9)$coef, 3)` (`r fp(vk(9)$p_value)`). Fifth, the timing is consistent with a price channel but does not establish it: the event-study coefficient peaks in 2022 (`r pp(es22$coef)`) and falls to `r pp(es23$coef)` in 2023, when Brent declined; a joint test does not reject that the `r nw(n_leads)` pre-shock coefficients are all zero (`r fp(wald_p)`), but it has little power; and the implicit subsidy, a falsification outcome, shows no differential (`r pp(t3$coef)`, `r fp(t3$p_value)`). Taken together, the results are suggestive of a larger subsidy response among net oil exporters, not conclusive.

The paper provides a transparent estimate, based on country-level data and a pre-specified treatment rule, of how a common oil price shock propagated differently across countries' budgets in a region with very heterogeneous exposure, and it links that estimate to a descriptive map of fiscal space. The policy analysis shows that pressure is not limited to exporters: several net importers combine high subsidies with high debt. Section 2 describes the context, data, and treatment definition; Section 3 presents descriptive evidence; Section 4 sets out a conceptual framework and the empirical strategy; Section 5 reports the results; Section 6 examines the identifying assumptions; Section 7 reports robustness checks, including the sensitivity to the definition of exporters, and discusses inference; Section 8 discusses budgetary implications and policy; and Section 9 concludes.

# Context and data

## The 2022 shock and the subsidy measures

The main data source is the IMF Fossil Fuel Subsidies Database [@imf2023ffsdata], documented in @black2023imf. It reports subsidies by country, year, fuel, and end use under the database's baseline scenario, and it separates two concepts. The *explicit* subsidy is the gap between the price paid by consumers and the cost of supply, multiplied by consumption; it is a budgetary or quasi-fiscal cost, and it responds mechanically to the international price when domestic prices are regulated. The *implicit* subsidy captures environmental and health externalities that are not priced, as well as forgone consumption taxes. It is dominated by slow-moving structural components such as consumption volumes and damage parameters.

The outcome variable of the analysis is the explicit subsidy as a percentage of GDP, because it is the component that should react to an international price shock in the short run. The implicit subsidy serves as a falsification outcome. It is an imperfect one: it is measured relative to the higher of the retail price and the supply cost, and it includes forgone value-added tax, so the two measures are constructed jointly and a price shock can move the implicit subsidy mechanically in either direction. I therefore read it as supporting evidence rather than as a formal test.

The shock variable is the annual average of the Europe Brent spot price [@eia2023brent], a series the IMF database does not include. In the `r y0`--`r y1` window, the 2022 increase of USD `r num(b_diff[["2022"]], 1)` per barrel is the largest year-on-year rise in dollar terms, and 2022 has the highest annual average. In percentage terms, the 2021 rebound from the pandemic trough was larger (`r sgn(b_2021_pct, 0)`%), which is one reason the design compares groups rather than years. In 2023 the price fell back to USD `r num(b_2023, 1)`.

## Fiscal variables

Fiscal indicators are sourced from the IMF World Economic Outlook, accessed via the IMF DataMapper API [@imf2023weo]: gross general government debt, the general government fiscal balance, and general government revenue, all expressed as a percent of GDP. I use the WEO rather than the World Bank because the policy analysis compares debt with subsidies country by country, which requires full coverage. The WEO series have `r if (weo_miss == 0) "no" else weo_miss` missing values for the `r n_c` countries over `r y0`--`r y1`. The corresponding World Bank series are missing for `r pct(min(wb_miss))` to `r pct(max(wb_miss))` of country-years depending on the indicator, with the gaps concentrated in the Caribbean, which would have reduced the fiscal comparison to a handful of cases.

The fiscal variables do not enter the DiD model. Debt, the fiscal balance, and revenue are themselves affected by the shock and by the subsidy; they are outcomes, not predetermined covariates, and conditioning on them would introduce bias. They are used only in the policy analysis of Section 8.

## Sample

The panel contains all `r n_c` LAC countries covered by the IMF database over `r y0`--`r y1`, giving `r n_obs` country-years. The window starts in 2015, the first year extracted from the database, and includes `r nw(n_pre)` pre-shock years (`r min(pre_years)`--`r max(pre_years)`) to assess parallel trends, the shock year (2022), and a reversal year (2023). Coverage of the explicit subsidy is nearly complete: the only missing values are for `r enum(miss_expl_c)` in `r min(miss_expl$anio)`--`r max(miss_expl$anio)`. Coverage of the implicit subsidy is less complete: it is missing for all years for `r enum(impl_none)`, and for most years for `r enum(impl_part)`, which matters for the falsification regression in Section 5.

## Treatment definition

Treatment status is defined by the net oil trade position, not by whether a country produces oil. What determines whether a government gains revenue when Brent rises is the net balance of oil trade. I fixed the classification rule before estimating any model: a country is a net oil exporter if its average net trade in crude oil and refined petroleum products (HS headings 2709 and 2710; exports minus imports in current USD, partner World) over 2015--2019 is positive, and a net oil importer otherwise. The trade data come from UN Comtrade [@uncomtrade]. Venezuela has not reported to Comtrade in any year of the window, so its position is rebuilt from mirror data, that is, from its partners' reported imports from and exports to Venezuela. Three countries reported only some years of the window (Haiti and St. Kitts and Nevis three, Dominica four); their averages use the years they reported, and all three are clearly net importers. The measure is taken before the shock and held fixed over time, so treatment status cannot respond to the 2022 price increase or to the subsidy response itself. The 2015--2019 window also ends before the pandemic and before Guyana's oil exports: production started in December 2019 and exports in 2020. Guyana was a net importer over the window and is classified as such; it appears as an exporter only in the 2019--2021 variant and in the earlier hand-coded list, both reported in Section 7.

The rule yields `r nw(n_exp)` net exporters, `r enum(exporters)`; the remaining `r n_imp` countries are net importers. Argentina illustrates why production is not the criterion: it exports some crude, but imports more refined products than it exports, so a higher Brent price raises the cost of supply more than it raises oil revenue. Two cases need comment. Puerto Rico does not appear in Comtrade, which records its trade under the United States, so the rule cannot be applied to it; I classify it as a net importer based on EIA data, which report that it has no crude oil production and no operating refinery [@eia2026pr]. Trinidad and Tobago is a knife-edge case: its average net oil trade is only USD `r num(tto_avg_m, 0)` million a year, negative in `r enum(tto_neg)` and positive in `r min(tto_pos)`--`r max(tto_pos)`, so a small change in the window could reclassify it. Section 7 reports the estimates without each of these two countries.

The data-based rule differs from the hand-coded list of `r nw(vk(5)$n_treated)` exporters used in an earlier version of this analysis in four countries. Mexico and Bolivia become net importers. Mexico's net crude exports (USD `r num(hs("MEX", 2709), 1)` billion a year) are outweighed by its net imports of refined products (USD `r num(-hs("MEX", 2710), 1)` billion). Bolivia's hydrocarbon exports are mainly natural gas (HS 2711), which the rule does not count, and its refined-product imports exceed its crude exports. Guyana becomes a net importer for the timing reason given above. Brazil becomes a net exporter, because its net crude exports (USD `r num(hs("BRA", 2709), 1)` billion a year) exceed its net imports of refined products (USD `r num(-hs("BRA", 2710), 1)` billion). I report the hand-coded list only as a sensitivity check, although it yields a smaller *p*-value than the main rule; a classification chosen after seeing the results would invalidate the inference. Table \ref{tab:countries} in Section 3 lists the classification with each country's explicit subsidy by year.

The treated group is small, and this shapes the rest of the analysis. With `r nw(n_exp)` exporters, standard errors are large, confidence intervals are wide, and conventional inference is fragile (see Section 7).

# Descriptive evidence

Figure \ref{fig:break} plots the explicit subsidy by group and year, in USD billion (panels a and b) and as a share of GDP (panels c and d). Between 2021 and 2022, the LAC total rose from USD `r num(cgv("LAC total", "usd_2021"), 1)` billion to USD `r num(cgv("LAC total", "usd_2022"), 1)` billion (`r sgn(cgv("LAC total", "change_usd_pct"), 1)`%), or from `r num(cgv("LAC total", "pct_gdp_2021"))`% to `r num(cgv("LAC total", "pct_gdp_2022"))`% of GDP. In these aggregates, the increase was not concentrated among exporters. Among net exporters, the subsidy went from `r num(cgv("Net exporter", "pct_gdp_2021"))`% to `r num(cgv("Net exporter", "pct_gdp_2022"))`% of GDP (`r pp(cgv("Net exporter", "change_pp"))`), while among net importers it went from `r num(cgv("Net importer", "pct_gdp_2021"))`% to `r num(cgv("Net importer", "pct_gdp_2022"))`% (`r pp(cgv("Net importer", "change_pp"))`; changes are computed from unrounded values). In dollar terms, exporters account for USD `r num(cgv("Net exporter", "change_usd_bn"), 1)` billion of the USD `r num(cgv("LAC total", "change_usd_bn"), 1)` billion increase. The series also shows the volatility of the pre-shock years, including the 2018 peak and the 2020 collapse, both of which reappear in the event study.

```{r break, results="asis"}
fig_float("fig1_break.png", "Explicit fossil fuel subsidies by exposure group, 2015--2023", "break", max_height = "0.64\\textheight")
```

Table \ref{tab:descriptive} reports the underlying numbers for the explicit, implicit, and total subsidy. The aggregates in Figure \ref{fig:break} and Table \ref{tab:descriptive} are group totals divided by group GDP, so large economies weigh more: Brazil, the largest exporter economy, has an explicit subsidy close to zero, and Mexico, the largest importer economy, saw its subsidy rise in 2022. The regressions in Section 5 weight every country equally, so a small economy with a large subsidy, such as Venezuela, counts as much as Brazil. The two approaches, therefore, give different pictures, and the differential estimated in Section 5 comes from the equal-weighted comparison. The implicit subsidy also rose in 2022 for both groups: from `r num(syv("Net exporters", 2021, "implicit_pct_gdp"))`% to `r num(syv("Net exporters", 2022, "implicit_pct_gdp"))`% of GDP among exporters and from `r num(syv("Net importers", 2021, "implicit_pct_gdp"))`% to `r num(syv("Net importers", 2022, "implicit_pct_gdp"))`% of GDP among importers. That increase is consistent with the price-sensitive tax component of the implicit measure and helps explain why the falsification outcome must be read with caution; the regression in Section 5 asks whether the implicit subsidy rose differentially among exporters once country and year effects are removed.

```{r tab-descriptive, results="asis"}
tab_float("tab1_descriptive.xlsx",
          paste0("Explicit, implicit and total subsidies by exposure group (USD billion and \\% of GDP), ", y0, "--", y1),
          "descriptive")
```

Table \ref{tab:countries} reports the explicit subsidy of each country by year, grouped by exposure, together with its change in 2022 relative to the 2015--2021 average. The levels are highly heterogeneous within both groups, ranging from Venezuela, whose subsidy ranged from `r num(min(ven_y), 1)`% to `r num(max(ven_y), 1)`% of GDP over `r y0`--`r y1`, to the `r nw(n_zero22)` countries, including Brazil, whose 2022 subsidy was at most `r num(im$floor_pct_gdp)`% of GDP.

```{r tab-countries, results="asis"}
tab_float("tab2_countries.xlsx",
          paste0("Classification of the ", n_c, " countries by net oil exposure and annual explicit subsidy (\\% of GDP)"),
          "countries", colsep = "4pt")
```

Figure \ref{fig:brent} connects the shock and the outcome. When the international price rises and is not passed through to consumers, the gap between supply cost and the regulated price widens, and the explicit subsidy grows almost mechanically. Over `r y0`--`r y1`, the Brent price and the aggregate explicit subsidy of LAC (in % of GDP) have a correlation of `r num(bt$corr_brent_explicit)`, with a joint peak in 2022. This correlation describes the link; it does not identify an effect. It pools exporters, where a higher price inflates the rent that finances the subsidy, with importers, where it raises the cost of supply, and it attributes to the price everything else that moved in the same years.

```{r brent, results="asis"}
fig_float("fig2_brent.png", "Brent price and aggregate explicit subsidy in LAC, 2015--2023", "brent", max_height = "0.52\\textheight")
```

Figure \ref{fig:impact} shows the change in the explicit subsidy by country, comparing 2022 with the 2015--2019 average, for the `r im$n_countries` countries whose subsidy exceeds `r num(im$floor_pct_gdp)`% of GDP in at least one year. Three pre-shock baselines appear in the paper, and each serves a different purpose. Figure \ref{fig:impact} uses 2015--2019 to exclude the pandemic years from the country-level comparison; Table \ref{tab:countries} and the DiD model use the full 2015--2021 pre-period; and Table \ref{tab:fiscal} reports the observed 2021--2022 change. `r if (same_top3) "The same three countries have the largest increases under the 2015--2019 and 2015--2021 baselines." else ""` The subsidy rose in `r im$n_increased` of the `r im$n_countries` countries`r if (length(tiny_up) > 0) paste0(" (in ", enum(tiny_up), " by less than 0.01 pp)") else ""`. The three largest increases are in `r enum(paste0(top3$country, " (", pp(top3$change_pp), ")"))`. `r Nw(length(top3_imp))` of the three, `r enum(top3_imp)`, are net importers, which already signals that fiscal pressure is not exclusive to exporters. Argentina, also a net importer, ranks `r ord(arg_rank)` (`r pp(imv("Argentina"))`), above `r nw(exp_below_arg)` of the `r nw(n_exp)` exporters. At the other end, `r enum(neg_exp)`, a net exporter whose explicit subsidy was close to zero throughout, recorded a marginal decrease (`r pp(imv(neg_exp[1]))`). The DiD estimate is an average differential between groups, not a description of each country's response, and this heterogeneity motivates two later choices: equal country weights in the model, and a country-by-country policy analysis in Section 8.
