
# Empirical strategy

## Conceptual framework

A simple accounting identity organizes the predictions. The explicit subsidy of country $i$ is the gap between the supply cost and the regulated consumer price, times the quantity consumed:
$$
ES_i = \left[c(P) - \bar p_i\right] Q_i,
$$
where $c(P)$ is the supply cost, increasing in the Brent price $P$, $\bar p_i$ is the regulated domestic price, and $Q_i$ is consumption. If $\bar p_i$ is sticky, an increase $dP$ raises $c(P)$ in every country, and the explicit subsidy rises everywhere, in importers as well as exporters. This common response is what the year effects of Section 4.3 absorb.

Exporters differ in one respect: they also receive oil rents $R_i(P)$, which rise with the price in proportion to net oil exports $N_i$. The windfall relaxes the government's budget constraint and makes it cheaper to hold $\bar p_i$ fixed rather than pass the price increase through to consumers. If $\pi_i$ denotes the share of the cost increase passed through, the change in the subsidy is approximately
$$
dES_i \approx (1 - \pi_i)\, c'(P)\, Q_i\, dP, \qquad \pi_i = \pi(N_i), \quad \pi'(N_i) < 0 .
$$
The prediction is a larger increase in the explicit subsidy among exporters ($N_i > 0$) than among importers, and a larger increase the larger the net oil exposure. The first part motivates the binary design used for the main estimate; the second motivates the continuous-exposure variant reported in Section 7.

This is a heuristic, not a structural model. It ignores, among other things, the political economy of price adjustment and differences in $Q_i$ and in the fuel mix. The most important omission is that pass-through also depends on the price-regulation regime, which differs across countries and is correlated with exporter status: a country with an administered price and a state-owned oil company may keep $\bar p_i$ fixed for reasons unrelated to its oil rents. The common response also varies with fuel intensity, $Q_i$ relative to GDP, so the year effects absorb only its average; if exporters or high-subsidy countries are more fuel-intensive, part of the differential reflects intensity rather than rents. The design cannot separate the rent channel from such differences in regimes and intensity, and the estimates below are a differential response by exporter status, not a test of the rent mechanism.

## Why difference-in-differences

The selection of method follows from the question and from the structure of the data. A before-and-after comparison of exporters does not isolate the shock, because other global elements also changed between 2021 and 2022, including the post-COVID-19 rebound and general inflation, and such a comparison would attribute all of them to the oil price. A comparison of exporters and importers in 2022 alone does not isolate it either, because the groups already differed before the shock: over 2015--2021, the average exporter's explicit subsidy was `r num(cell("Net exporter", "pre_2015_2021"))`% of GDP, compared with `r num(cell("Net importer", "pre_2015_2021"))`% for the average importer. The data, however, have two dimensions, time and group. Net importers went through the same period and faced the same price increase, but without the oil-rent channel. Comparing the change in exporters with the change in importers is a difference-in-differences comparison [@angrist2009mostly]. Because importers are also exposed, the comparison does not recover what exporters' subsidies would have been without the shock; it recovers how much more they rose than those of a lower-exposure group with identical timing.

## Specification

Let $S_{it}$ denote the explicit subsidy of country $i$ in year $t$, in percent of GDP. The baseline $2\times 2$ regression is
$$
S_{it} = \beta_0 + \beta_1\,\text{Post}_t + \beta_2\,\text{Exporter}_i + \beta_3\,(\text{Post}_t \times \text{Exporter}_i) + \varepsilon_{it},
$$
where $\text{Post}_t = 1$ in 2022 and $\text{Exporter}_i = 1$ for the `r nw(n_exp)` net exporters. The main specification replaces the group and period terms with country and year fixed effects:
$$
S_{it} = \beta_3\,(\text{Post}_t \times \text{Exporter}_i) + \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \varepsilon_{it}.
$$
The country effects $\alpha_i$ absorb everything that is constant within a country, including exporter status and the level of its subsidy regime. The year effects $\lambda_t$ absorb the part of common shocks, such as the level of the Brent price, the pandemic, and the regional business cycle, that affects all countries equally; any response to them that differs systematically between exporters and importers is not absorbed and loads on $\beta_3$. The coefficient $\beta_3$ measures the change in exporters' subsidy between the 2015--2021 average and 2022, in excess of the corresponding change among importers. Because importers are also exposed to the price increase, $\beta_3$ is the difference between the shock's effect on exporters and its effect on importers; the latter is absorbed by the 2022 year effect and is not identified.

The outcome is measured in percentage points of GDP, and parallel trends is assumed on that scale. Because exporters start from a much higher level, a proportional version of the assumption would imply a different differential; and because exporters' GDP also rises with the oil price, part of any response in the numerator is offset in the ratio.

The static regressions use `r sub("-", "--", smp$static_years)`: `r nw(n_pre)` pre-shock years and the shock year. The year 2023 is excluded from the static estimator because Brent had already fallen and pooling it with 2022 would average a shock year with a reversal year. It is kept in the event study, which shows whether the differential reverses. Each country receives equal weight. Standard errors are clustered by country, which allows arbitrary serial correlation within countries. With `r nw(n_exp)` treated clusters out of `r n_c`, however, conventional cluster-robust standard errors tend to be too small, and the reported *p*-values should be read as lower bounds [@cameron2008bootstrap; @mackinnon2017wild]. Methods designed for this case, namely the wild cluster restricted bootstrap, randomization inference that reassigns exporter status across the `r n_c` countries, and the procedure of @conley2011inference, are the appropriate next step; I expect them to widen rather than narrow the confidence interval.

For the event study, I replace the single interaction with one interaction per year,
$$
S_{it} = \sum_{k \neq `r base_year`} \delta_k\,\mathbf{1}[t = k]\times\text{Exporter}_i + \alpha_i + \lambda_t + \varepsilon_{it},
$$
estimated on `r sub("-", "--", smp$event_study_years)`, with `r base_year`, the last pre-shock year, as the reference. The coefficients $\delta_{2015},\allowbreak\dots,\allowbreak\delta_{2020}$ are `r nw(n_leads)` leads that trace the pre-shock gap between groups; $\delta_{2022}$ is the shock-year differential and $\delta_{2023}$ the differential one year later.

# Results

## The $2\times 2$ comparison

The DiD estimate can be read directly from four group means (unweighted country-years). Among net exporters, the explicit subsidy averaged `r num(cell("Net exporter", "pre_2015_2021"))`% of GDP in 2015--2021 and `r num(cell("Net exporter", "post_2022"))`% in 2022, an increase of `r npp(dd$exporter_change)`. Among net importers, it went from `r num(cell("Net importer", "pre_2015_2021"))`% to `r num(cell("Net importer", "post_2022"))`%, an increase of `r npp(dd$importer_change)`. Importers' subsidies therefore also rose, which is why the double difference, `r pp(dd$double_difference)` of GDP, is a differential rather than a total effect. The four cells contain `r cell_n("Net exporter", "pre_2015_2021")`, `r cell_n("Net exporter", "post_2022")`, `r cell_n("Net importer", "pre_2015_2021")` and `r cell_n("Net importer", "post_2022")` observations; the total of `r t1$n_obs` reflects the missing Puerto Rico observations noted in Section 2.

## Two-way fixed effects estimates

Table \ref{tab:model} reports the regression estimates. Column (1) reproduces the $2\times 2$ comparison as a regression: $\hat\beta_3 = `r num(t1$coef)`$ (SE `r num(t1$se)`, `r fp(t1$p_value)`). Column (2), the main specification with country and year fixed effects, gives `r npp(t2$coef)` of GDP (SE `r num(t2$se)`, `r fp(t2$p_value)`, 95% CI `r fci(t2$ci_low, t2$ci_high)`). The two estimates nearly coincide, as they must in a design with a single treatment date and a nearly balanced panel; column (1) shows where the TWFE coefficient comes from, and their agreement is not evidence of robustness. The point estimate is economically meaningful, about `r pct(b3_share)` of the average pre-shock subsidy of exporters, but it is not statistically significant at conventional levels, and its 95% confidence interval includes both zero and differentials more than twice as large as the point estimate. With `r nw(t2$n_treated)` treated countries, and with the few-cluster problem discussed in Section 4, this *p*-value is more likely to be too small than too large. This is the main, pre-specified result, and I report it as such rather than searching for a classification or specification that yields a smaller \textit{p}-value; Section 7 reports the alternatives.

```{r tab-model, results="asis"}
tab_float("tab3_model.xlsx",
          "Differential response of subsidies to the 2022 shock, net oil exporters relative to net oil importers: difference-in-differences estimates",
          "model")
```

## Auxiliary outcomes: implicit and total subsidy

If the estimated differential reflects the price channel, it should appear in the explicit subsidy, which is a price gap, more than in the implicit subsidy, which is dominated by structural components. Column (3) estimates the same TWFE model with the implicit subsidy as the dependent variable. The coefficient is `r pp(t3$coef)` of GDP (SE `r num(t3$se)`, `r fp(t3$p_value)`, 95% CI `r fci(t3$ci_low, t3$ci_high)`): negative and far from significant. The implicit subsidy is not independent of the explicit one, however: it is measured relative to the higher of the retail price and the supply cost and includes forgone VAT, so a price shock can move it mechanically in either direction. The null result is therefore consistent with, but does not isolate, a price channel, and its confidence interval admits differential effects of up to `r npp(t3$ci_high)`. Because the explicit differential is itself not significant, the contrast between the two outcomes is weaker evidence than it would otherwise be. The sample also differs: the falsification regression has `r t3$n_countries` countries and `r t3$n_obs` observations because the implicit subsidy is missing for `r enum(impl_none)` and partly for `r enum(impl_part)`, so columns (2) and (3) are not estimated on the same countries. Column (4) uses the total subsidy: `r npp(t4$coef)` (SE `r num(t4$se)`, `r fp(t4$p_value)`). It is close in magnitude to the explicit differential and, like it, not statistically significant; because the samples differ and the IMF total is computed separately from its components, columns (2)--(4) need not add up.

# Identification checks

## Parallel trends

The identifying assumption of the static estimator is that, absent the difference in exposure, the explicit subsidy of exporters and importers would have changed by the same amount between the pre-shock average and 2022:
$$
\mathbb{E}\left[S^0_{i,2022}-\bar S^0_{i,\text{pre}}\mid \text{Exporter}_i=1\right] = \mathbb{E}\left[S^0_{i,2022}-\bar S^0_{i,\text{pre}}\mid \text{Exporter}_i=0\right],
$$
where $\bar S^0_{i,\text{pre}}$ is the 2015--2021 average, and $S^0$ is the subsidy that exporters would have had with an importer-type exposure. The event study uses the same condition with 2021 in place of the pre-shock average. The assumption cannot be tested directly, but the event study shows whether the two groups were already separating before 2022. Figure \ref{fig:eventstudy} plots the coefficients.

```{r eventstudy, results="asis"}
fig_float("fig4_eventstudy.png", "Event study: differential response of the explicit subsidy by year (base year 2021)", "eventstudy", max_height = "0.52\\textheight")
```

The `r nw(n_leads)` pre-shock coefficients are `r enum(paste0(sgn(es_pre$coef), " (", es_pre$year, ")"))`. `r Nw(sum(pre_cover0))` of their 95% confidence intervals include zero; the exception is `r pre_excl0$year`, whose lower bound is barely above zero (`r num(pre_excl0$ci_low)`). The largest coefficient appears in 2022 ($\hat\delta_{2022} = `r sgn(es22$coef)`$, 95% CI `r fci(es22$ci_low, es22$ci_high)`), and it declines in 2023 ($\hat\delta_{2023} = `r sgn(es23$coef)`$, 95% CI `r fci(es23$ci_low, es23$ci_high)`), in line with the fall in oil prices. Neither interval excludes zero.

A joint Wald test does not reject the null that the `r nw(n_leads)` leads are all zero: $F(`r wald$df1`, `r wald_df2`) = `r num(wald$f_stat)`$, `r fp(wald_p)`, with the denominator degrees of freedom set to the number of clusters minus one. This is weak support for parallel trends, not a validation. With `r nw(n_exp)` treated clusters and lead standard errors of up to `r npp(se_max_lead)`, the test has little power against pre-trends of the size of the estimated effect, and conditioning the analysis on passing such a pre-test can itself distort estimates and inference [@roth2022pretest]. With a single post-period, $\beta_3$ also cannot separate the response to the shock from any other exporter-specific shock in 2022: a group-specific deviation of the size seen before 2022 would enter the point estimate directly rather than only widening its confidence interval [@conley2011inference].

The pattern of the leads matters for interpretation. `r Nw(n_pre_pos)` of the `r nw(n_leads)` are positive; only `r enum(pre_neg)` is negative. Relative to 2021, the exporter--importer gap was therefore larger in most earlier years, and the reference year is a comparatively low point for exporters. In the aggregates of Table \ref{tab:descriptive}, importers' subsidies rebounded more than exporters' between 2020 and 2021. This is why $\hat\delta_{2022}$, measured against 2021, is larger than the static $\hat\beta_3$ (`r npp(t2$coef)`), which is measured against the 2015--2021 average. The leads also co-move with the Brent price: over `r min(lp$year)`--`r max(lp$year)`, their correlation with the annual Brent average is `r num(r_leads_brent)`, and the largest lead, `r sgn(d_top)` in `r lead_top`, falls in the pre-shock year with the highest price among the lead years. The reference year does not fit this pattern: Brent in 2021 (USD `r num(brent_ref, 1)`) was close to its `r lead_top` level (USD `r num(brent_top, 1)`), yet the gap was, by construction, zero, and including the 2021 point lowers the correlation to `r num(r_lead_brent)`. Measured against `r lead_top` rather than 2021, the 2022 differential would be `r pp(d2022_vs_top)`. The leads are thus consistent with exporters' subsidies responding somewhat more to the oil price every year, in which case the pre-period is not an untreated baseline, but seven points with one discordant year cannot establish such a pattern. I read $\beta_3$ as the differential response to an unusually large price increase, estimated with considerable uncertainty and sensitive to the choice of the pre-shock benchmark.

A formal sensitivity analysis that bounds post-period violations of parallel trends by the size of pre-period violations [@rambachan2023more] is a natural extension. Because the 95% interval for $\delta_{2022}$ already includes zero, such an analysis could only widen it.

## No anticipation

The second premise is that exporters' subsidies in 2021 did not respond to a shock that had not yet occurred. With a sole shock year, this assumption cannot be tested with the data, and I do not claim to have validated it. The argument is institutional: the invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 was unanticipated, and there is no indication that any government in the region repositioned its fuel subsidies in 2021 in expectation of a price increase in 2022. The leads show no sign of an anticipatory rise among exporters: in 2021 the exporter--importer gap was smaller than in `r nw(n_pre_pos)` of the `r nw(n_leads)` earlier years. The more relevant concern is that prices were already rising in 2021, so the base year is partly exposed. To the extent that the 2021 differential response has the same sign as the 2022 one, this biases the 2022 coefficient toward zero rather than away from it.

## No spillovers

The design also assumes that one country's treatment status does not affect subsidies in another, the stable unit treatment value assumption. Regional energy trade could violate it. Venezuela and Trinidad and Tobago supply crude oil and refined products to Caribbean neighbours, and Colombia and Ecuador trade fuels with their neighbours, so the terms on which exporters supply the region can shift the supply cost, and hence the explicit subsidy, of importers. Flows can also run the other way: Bolivia, a net oil importer under the main rule, sells natural gas to Argentina and to Brazil, a treated country, so a comparison country's windfall can affect a treated one, which could bias $\beta_3$ in either direction. Spillovers that affect all countries equally are absorbed by the year effects; only those that fall differently on the two groups bias $\beta_3$. If exporters shared part of their 2022 windfall with importing neighbours through cheaper supply, importers' subsidies would rise less than they otherwise would, and $\beta_3$ would overstate the differential. If exporters instead cut supply to neighbours when prices rose, importers' costs would rise more, and $\beta_3$ would understate it. The direction of the bias is therefore ambiguous, and with country-level annual data, the assumption cannot be tested here.

# Robustness \& inference

## Extreme cases and leave-one-out

Two countries are extreme in the distribution of the outcome. Venezuela's explicit subsidy reached `r num(rb$max_subsidy_pct_gdp$venezuela, 1)`% of GDP in 2022, the highest among exporters, and Suriname's reached `r num(rb$max_subsidy_pct_gdp$suriname, 1)`%, the highest among importers. Dropping Venezuela from the main specification would amount to selecting on the outcome, so I keep it and instead report the main TWFE specification on alternative samples in Table \ref{tab:robustness}. Without Venezuela, the estimate falls from `r num(t2$coef)` to `r num(nven$coef)` (SE `r num(nven$se)`, `r fp(nven$p_value)`, 95% CI `r fci(nven$ci_low, nven$ci_high)`). This is the most consequential sensitivity in the paper: most of the point estimate comes from one country, which is also the country whose GDP, the denominator of the outcome, is most uncertain after hyperinflation. Excluding Suriname raises the estimate to `r num(exr("without_suriname")$coef)` (SE `r num(exr("without_suriname")$se)`, `r fp(exr("without_suriname")$p_value)`), because it removes a large-subsidy importer from the comparison group. Excluding both yields `r num(exr("without_both")$coef)` (SE `r num(exr("without_both")$se)`, `r fp(exr("without_both")$p_value)`).

```{r tab-robustness, results="asis"}
tab_float("tab4_robustness.xlsx",
          "Sensitivity of $\\beta_3$ to the exclusion of extreme cases",
          "robustness")
```

A systematic version of the same exercise drops each of the `r nw(rb$n_exporters)` exporters in turn. The coefficient remains positive in every case, ranging from `r num(rb$loo_range$min)` (without `r rb$loo_range$country_at_min`) to `r num(rb$loo_range$max)` (without `r rb$loo_range$country_at_max`), and none of the `r nw(nrow(loo))` estimates is significant at the 10% level. Dropping Brazil raises the estimate because its explicit subsidy is close to zero throughout and fell marginally in 2022. These re-estimates have only `r nw(n_exp - 1)` treated clusters and inherit the inference problem discussed below. The sign of the differential does not hinge on a single country; its size does, and it hinges on Venezuela. The exercise drops only treated units; dropping comparison countries one at a time would show whether the composition of the comparison group matters, and is a further extension.

## Sensitivity to the definition of exporters

Table \ref{tab:classification} re-estimates the main specification under alternative definitions of exporters. Panel A reports the variants that were specified together with the main rule, before estimation; Panel B reports three variants that I added after inspecting the classification and the continuous-exposure result, and they should be read as post hoc. Row (1) reproduces the main estimate.

```{r tab-classification, results="asis"}
tab_float("tab5_classification.xlsx",
          "Sensitivity of $\\beta_3$ to the definition of net oil exporters",
          "classification", colsep = "4pt")
```

Every binary definition gives a positive point estimate, between `r num(min(bin$coef))` and `r num(max(bin$coef))`, and none is significant at the 5% level. Adding petroleum gases (row 2) moves `r iso2c(cs$switches$v2_gas$to_exporter)` to the exporter group and gives the largest binary estimate, `r num(vk(2)$coef)` (`r fp(vk(2)$p_value)`, with a 95% CI whose lower end is essentially zero). Bolivia's classification matters because its subsidy rose by `r npp(bol_ch)` in 2022 relative to its 2015--2021 average, the second-largest increase in the sample; as a gas exporter, it also received a windfall that the main rule does not count. Averaging over 2019--2021 (row 3) moves `r iso2c(cs$switches$v3_1921$to_exporter)` to the exporter group and gives `r num(vk(3)$coef)` (`r fp(vk(3)$p_value)`); dropping Guyana (row 4) leaves the main estimate almost unchanged (`r num(vk(4)$coef)`). The hand-coded list used in the earlier version of this analysis (row 5) gives `r num(vk(5)$coef)` (`r fp(vk(5)$p_value)`). I report it only as a sensitivity check: the rule in row (1) was fixed before estimation, and choosing among classifications after seeing their *p*-values would invalidate the inference. Dropping Puerto Rico (row 7) or Trinidad and Tobago (row 8), the two cases that rest on an outside source or a near-zero average, leaves the estimate positive and not significant (`r num(vk(7)$coef)` and `r num(vk(8)$coef)`). The sign of the differential is robust to how exporters are defined; its statistical significance is not.

Row (6) replaces the binary indicator with net oil trade as a percentage of GDP (2015--2019 average), interacted with $\text{Post}_t$. Each additional percentage point of GDP in net oil exports is associated with a `r num(vk(6)$coef, 3)`\ pp larger increase in the explicit subsidy in 2022 (SE `r num(vk(6)$se, 3)`, `r fp(vk(6)$p_value)`). This is the dose--response pattern predicted in Section 4.1: the larger the net oil exposure, the larger the differential response. I treat it as complementary evidence, not as the main result, for three reasons. First, the exposure distribution is highly skewed. Net oil trade ranges from `r num(ex_dist$min, 1)`% of GDP (`r e_min_c`) to `r num(ex_dist$max, 1)`% (`r e_max_c`), with a median of `r num(ex_dist$median, 1)`%, and `r n_e_neg` of the `r nrow(ebc)` countries have negative values; Venezuela's exposure is more than four times that of the next country, `r e_2nd_c` (`r num(ex_dist$second, 1)`%). The slope is therefore heavily leveraged by one country: without Venezuela (row 9, post hoc), it falls to `r num(vk(9)$coef, 3)` (SE `r num(vk(9)$se, 3)`, `r fp(vk(9)$p_value)`), `r pct(cont_drop)` lower. Second, with `r vk(6)$n_countries` clusters and one high-leverage cluster, clustered standard errors are likely too small [@mackinnon2017wild], so the *p*-value overstates the precision. Third, the continuous variant was pre-specified as a sensitivity check, not as the main specification, and promoting it after seeing that it is significant would be the kind of specification search the pre-specified rule is meant to prevent. I read it as suggestive evidence of a dose--response pattern that survives, in attenuated form, the exclusion of Venezuela.

## Inference with few treated clusters

The small treated group is the main limitation of the design, and it affects inference in two ways. First, with `r nw(n_exp)` treated clusters, conventional cluster-robust standard errors understate variability because the variance of $\hat\beta_3$ is driven by the few treated clusters [@cameron2008bootstrap; @mackinnon2017wild], so the *p*-values in Tables \ref{tab:model}, \ref{tab:robustness}, and \ref{tab:classification} are likely optimistic. This reinforces, rather than overturns, the conclusion that the binary estimates are not statistically significant. Second, idiosyncratic shocks to `r nw(n_exp)` countries do not average out: the estimator does not concentrate around the true differential as the number of comparison countries grows [@conley2011inference], so any single estimate can be far from the true value even if it is correct on average. The dependence on Venezuela is a concrete instance of this problem. The wild cluster restricted bootstrap, randomization inference over exporter status, and the @conley2011inference procedure address these problems and are the natural next step; I have not run them, and I expect them to widen the confidence intervals. The recent econometric literature on DiD also discusses the interpretation of pre-trend tests and the problems of TWFE in the context of staggered adoption [@roth2023trending]. The last concern does not arise here, because treatment starts in the same year for every treated country, so the TWFE estimator reduces to a comparison between one high-exposure cohort and a lower-exposure comparison group with identical timing.

# Budgetary implications and policy

## A subsidy--debt matrix

The estimate in Section 5 is an average differential; the policy question is where the subsidy is most costly relative to the fiscal room to sustain it. I build a descriptive matrix of the `r fa$n_countries` countries with an explicit subsidy exceeding `r num(fa$subsidy_floor_pct_gdp)`% of GDP in 2022 (`r fa$n_exporters` exporters and `r fa$n_importers` importers). `r enum(exp_out)`, the remaining exporter, is not in the matrix: its explicit subsidy was `r num(bra22)`% of GDP in 2022, below the floor. The horizontal axis shows the explicit subsidy in 2022, and the vertical axis shows gross public debt in 2022, both expressed as a percent of GDP. The sample medians, `r num(fa$median_subsidy_pct_gdp)`% of GDP for the subsidy and `r num(fa$median_debt_pct_gdp, 1)`% of GDP for debt, divide the plane into four quadrants. I use medians rather than means because they are not driven by extreme values such as Venezuela. Fiscal space is proxied by the debt stock rather than the one-year deficit, which is volatile and cyclical. The matrix is a prioritization device, not a causal model: it indicates where reform is most pressing, not the effect of any particular policy. Figure \ref{fig:matrix} shows the matrix and Table \ref{tab:fiscal} reports the underlying values.

```{r matrix, results="asis"}
fig_float("fig5_fiscal_matrix.png", "Subsidy--debt matrix and policy quadrants, 2022", "matrix", max_height = "0.76\\textheight")
```

The *urgent reform* quadrant (subsidy and debt both above the median) contains `r nw(nrow(urg))` countries: `r enum(the_c(qc[["Urgent reform"]]))`. It mixes `r nw(length(urg_exp))` exporters (`r enum(urg_exp)`) with `r nw(length(urg_imp))` importers (`r enum(urg_imp)`). Venezuela combines a subsidy of `r num(fcv("Venezuela", "explicit_subsidy_pct_gdp_2022"), 1)`% of GDP with debt of `r num(fcv("Venezuela", "debt_pct_gdp_2022"), 1)`% of GDP, Suriname `r num(fcv("Suriname", "explicit_subsidy_pct_gdp_2022"), 1)`% with `r num(fcv("Suriname", "debt_pct_gdp_2022"), 1)`%, and Bolivia `r num(fcv("Bolivia", "explicit_subsidy_pct_gdp_2022"), 1)`% with `r num(fcv("Bolivia", "debt_pct_gdp_2022"), 1)`%. `r Nw(nrow(urg_def))` of the `r nw(nrow(urg))` also ran a fiscal deficit in 2022, the largest in `r urg_def$country[1]` (`r num(urg_def$fiscal_balance_pct_gdp_2022[1], 1)`% of GDP) and `r urg_def$country[2]` (`r num(urg_def$fiscal_balance_pct_gdp_2022[2], 1)`%). The *gradual reform* quadrant (high subsidy, debt below the median) contains `r enum(the_c(qc[["Gradual reform"]]))`, again a mix of exporters and importers. The *monitor* quadrant (low subsidy, high debt) contains `r enum(the_c(qc[["Monitor"]]))`, all small Caribbean economies with limited fiscal room. The *no immediate pressure* quadrant contains `r enum(the_c(qc[["No immediate pressure"]]))`. The cut-offs are sample medians, and some countries sit close to them: `r enum(the_c(near_med))` are within `r band_debt` points of GDP of the debt median or within `r num(band_sub, 1)`\ pp of the subsidy median, and could change quadrant under small changes in the thresholds.

```{r tab-fiscal, results="asis"}
tab_float("tab6_fiscal.xlsx",
          "Subsidy, illustrative differential cost and fiscal space by country, 2022",
          "fiscal", colsep = "5pt")
```

As an illustration only, Table \ref{tab:fiscal} values the average differential of `r npp(t2$coef)` of GDP at the 2022 GDP of each of the `r nw(nrow(fx))` exporters in the matrix. The figure is how much more an exporter of that size would have spent than an importer-type response implies, *if* it responded like the average exporter. It is neither the total cost of the shock nor the country's realized cost, and it inherits the uncertainty of $\hat\beta_3$, whose 95% CI of `r fci(t2$ci_low, t2$ci_high)` includes zero, so the lower end of every range is negative. For Colombia, the largest of these economies, the valuation is USD `r num(fxv("Colombia", "cost"), 1)` billion, with a range of USD `r num(fxv("Colombia", "cost_lo"), 1)` billion to USD `r num(fxv("Colombia", "cost_hi"), 1)` billion across the confidence interval, compared with a realized 2021--2022 increase of USD `r num(fxv("Colombia", "change_usd_bn_2021_2022"), 1)` billion; for Ecuador it is USD `r num(fxv("Ecuador", "cost"), 1)` billion (range `r num(fxv("Ecuador", "cost_lo"), 1)` to `r num(fxv("Ecuador", "cost_hi"), 1)`), and for Venezuela, whose GDP is the most uncertain, USD `r num(fxv("Venezuela", "cost"), 2)` billion. No figure is reported for importers: they are the comparison group, so their differential is zero by construction, and the model identifies nothing about the shock's cost for them, which is absorbed by the year effects. The observed change is shown in a separate column (in pp); its absolute value in USD billion sets the size of the points in Figure \ref{fig:matrix}, with hollow points for decreases.

The main lesson of the matrix is that fiscal pressure from fuel subsidies does not align with the oil trade position. Whatever the size of the average differential, importers such as `r enum(intersect(c("Suriname", "Bolivia", "Argentina"), urg_imp))` are among the most exposed. High subsidies combined with high debt were present before 2022 and, in the raw data, rose further in several of these countries in 2022 (Table \ref{tab:countries}); the model does not identify how much of that rise in importers is due to the shock.

## Regressivity and the case for targeted compensation

Removing a subsidy raises fuel prices and lowers households' real income, so the policy question is not whether to reform but how to protect low-income households during the transition. Universal fuel subsidies are a poorly targeted instrument. Because benefits are proportional to consumption, which rises with income, they accrue mostly to richer households: for developing countries, @coady2015unequal find that the richest income quintile captures more than 40% of the benefits of fuel subsidies, about six times the share of the poorest quintile. Replacing universal price subsidies with targeted transfers to vulnerable households can improve equity and free up fiscal space by ending transfers to higher-income households. A well-designed reform need not be regressive.

## A differentiated reform sequence

The recommendation varies by quadrant. In the urgent reform quadrant, domestic price adjustment should come first, accompanied by immediate targeted compensation; several of these countries already run deficits, and there is little room to postpone the adjustment. In the gradual reform quadrant, lower debt allows a phased transition with an announced schedule and compensation for vulnerable households. In the monitor and no-immediate-pressure quadrants, the priority is surveillance: because the explicit subsidy rises with oil prices, a new price shock can move these countries toward the urgent reform quadrant. Across all groups, a common sequence applies, compressed in time for the urgent reform quadrant: first, adopt a pricing rule that passes international price changes through to domestic prices, with smoothing if needed; second, close the remaining price gap on an announced path; third, redirect the savings to targeted transfers.

# Conclusion

Under a treatment rule fixed before estimation, the explicit fossil fuel subsidy of LAC net oil exporters rose by about `r npp(t2$coef)` of GDP more than that of net importers in 2022. The estimate is imprecise and not statistically significant (`r fp(t2$p_value)`; 95% CI `r fci(t2$ci_low, t2$ci_high)`), and with `r nw(n_exp)` treated countries, conventional clustered standard errors are likely too small, so the true uncertainty is larger than reported. Importers were also exposed to the shock, so this is a differential response, not the total effect of the shock. The point estimate is positive under every binary definition of exporters considered (`r num(min(bin$coef))` to `r npp(max(bin$coef))`) and when each exporter is dropped in turn, so its sign is robust; its size is not, since it falls to `r npp(nven$coef)` without Venezuela. A continuous measure of net oil exposure points in the same direction, with a larger differential response the larger a country's net oil exports, but it is heavily leveraged by Venezuela and was pre-specified only as a sensitivity check. The timing is consistent with a price channel: the differential peaks in 2022 and falls in 2023 as oil prices decline, and the implicit subsidy shows no statistically significant differential response. The joint pre-trend test does not reject, but it has little power, and the leads co-move with the Brent price before 2021. The main caveats are the small treated group and the weight of one country; the confounding of exporter status with price-regulation regimes; possible spillovers through regional energy trade; and a falsification outcome that is not independent of the explicit measure. Overall, the evidence is suggestive of a larger subsidy response among net oil exporters, not conclusive.

These caveats point to concrete extensions: small-cluster and leverage-robust inference (wild cluster restricted bootstrap, randomization inference, and the @conley2011inference procedure), which matters most for the continuous-exposure estimate; a sensitivity analysis for violations of parallel trends [@rambachan2023more]; a design that interacts net oil exposure with the Brent price in every year; and direct measures of price-regulation regimes, which would help separate the oil-rent channel from differences in pricing institutions.

The fiscal analysis shows that high subsidies combined with high debt are not limited to exporters. For importers, a subsidy tied to the international price expands exactly when supply is most expensive; for exporters, it absorbs the oil windfall that could otherwise be saved. In both cases, it is procyclical. Reforming it, in a sequence adapted to each country's fiscal space and with targeted compensation in place of universal price support, would free fiscal resources and reduce the exposure of public finances to oil price volatility.
